module_contract.goal: Score atrophy against the patient's age, separate the neurodegenerative phenotypes on MRI, recognise the hydrocephalus that may respond to shunting, and run ARIA surveillance on anti-amyloid therapy.

source.title: Dementia — Role of MRI and Visual Rating Scales

approach.detail: Coronal T1 at the level of the anterior pons through the body of the hippocampus. Score each side separately.

approach.step: Read that score against the patient's age
approach.detail: The same MTA grade is normal at 80 and abnormal at 65. Never report the grade without the age threshold beside it.
GCA across the whole brain on T1; Koedam on sagittal, coronal and axial, taking the highest of the three planes.
Fazekas on transverse FLAIR or T2. Distinguish the punctate lesions of normal ageing from beginning confluence.
T2* or SWI for lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — amyloid angiopathy, and the baseline for any anti-amyloid therapy.
Asymmetry, frontal or temporal pole predominance, midbrain or pontine atrophy, putaminal signal — these separate the syndromes that the scales cannot.

classify.name: MTA — medial temporal atrophy (coronal T1, anterior pons level)
rows: Widening of the choroid fissure only
Widening of the choroid fissure and the temporal horn
Under 75: abnormal on at least one side. 75 and over: abnormal if bilateral
Moderate loss of hippocampal volume — reduced height
Severe volume loss of the hippocampus
classify.note: Cut-offs: under 75 years, mean score ≥ 1.5 is abnormal; 75 and over, ≥ 2.0. Score each hemisphere separately — asymmetry of more than 2 points argues against Alzheimer's and towards FTLD.

measure.cutoff: 0 none · 1 opening of sulci · 2 volume loss of gyri · 3 end-stage knife-blade

measure.how: Sagittal, coronal and axial T1; take the highest score of the three planes. Look at the posterior cingulate and parieto-occipital sulci and the precuneus.
measure.cutoff: 0 closed sulci · 1 mild widening · 2 substantial · 3 end-stage knife-blade

measure.what: Fazekas — white matter hyperintensity (score the two arms separately)
measure.how: Periventricular and deep white matter are graded on separate 0–3 scales; report both, because an unqualified "Fazekas 2" is ambiguous.
measure.cutoff: Periventricular: 0 none · 1 caps or thin lining · 2 smooth halo · 3 irregular, extending into deep white matter. Deep: 0 none · 1 punctate · 2 beginning confluence · 3 large confluent

measure.how: A normal medial temporal lobe does not exclude the diagnosis, but it makes it less likely.
Worth stating in the report, because it changes what the clinic does next.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
MRI brain, dementia protocol: 3D T1, transverse FLAIR, T2*/SWI[, DWI].

FINDINGS
MTA: right [0–4], left [0–4]. [Normal / abnormal] for age [n].
GCA: [0–3].
Koedam (posterior cortical atrophy): [0–3].
Fazekas: [0–3]. Lacunar infarcts: [none / n, sites].
Microbleeds on SWI: [none / n, lobar or deep]. Superficial siderosis: [absent / present].
Regional: frontal and temporal pole [symmetric / asymmetric], midbrain [normal / atrophic], pons and cerebellum [ ], putamen [ ].
Hippocampal asymmetry: [n points].

IMPRESSION
1. [Pattern: medial temporal predominant / posterior predominant / frontotemporal / vascular / normal for age].
2. Scores: MTA [ ] (abnormal for age [yes/no]), GCA [ ], Koedam [ ], Fazekas [ ].
3. [Amyloid angiopathy features, if present.]
4. [Suggested correlation or functional imaging.]
pitfalls: Reporting MTA without the age. Score ≥ 1.5 is abnormal under 75 but ≥ 2.0 is the threshold at 75 and over — the same picture changes meaning.
Scoring MTA off an oblique coronal. It is scored at the level of the anterior pons through the body of the hippocampus, and a tilted slice inflates the grade.
Calling Fazekas 1 disease. Multiple punctate lesions are normal in the elderly; confluence beginning to bridge is where it becomes pathological.
Missing posterior cortical atrophy because you only scored one plane. Koedam is scored on sagittal, coronal and axial, and you take the highest.
Calling a normal hippocampus 'no dementia'. In dementia with Lewy bodies the hippocampus is typically normal — that is the finding, not its absence.
Ignoring marked left-right asymmetry. More than 2 points of difference argues away from Alzheimer's and towards frontotemporal degeneration.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with two years of progressive episodic memory loss. On coronal T1 angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, the choroid fissures are widened, the temporal horns enlarged and the hippocampal height reduced, giving a medial temporal atrophy score of 2 on each side. Posterior atrophy is 0 and the frontal lobes look normal. What do you report?
quiz.answer: Medial temporal atrophy beyond the age cut-off, a pattern that supports Alzheimer disease
choices: Medial temporal atrophy beyond the age cut-off, a pattern that supports Alzheimer disease
Medial temporal atrophy still within the expected range at this age, so a normal study
Global cortical atrophy out of proportion to the rest, favouring a vascular contribution
Posterior-predominant atrophy out of keeping with the age, favouring a parietal syndrome
quiz.explain: The Scheltens medial temporal atrophy (MTA) scale runs 0 to 4 and is read on a coronal T1 angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, weighing three things together: width of the choroid fissure, width of the temporal horn, and height of the hippocampal formation. The score only means something once you attach an age. The cut-off in common use is a score of 2 or more below the age of 75, and 3 or more at 75 and above; scoring without that adjustment is how normal ageing gets reported as disease. At 68 with a score of 2 bilaterally this study sits above the threshold, and in an amnestic presentation that supports Alzheimer disease. The other readings do not fit what was measured: global cortical atrophy and frontal change were not present, and the posterior atrophy score was 0.

quiz.prompt: On an axial CT slice through the frontal horns, the maximal width across the frontal horns is 42 mm and the maximal internal diameter of the skull on the same slice is 130 mm. Calculate the Evans index. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The Evans index is the maximal width across the frontal horns divided by the maximal internal diameter of the inner table on the same axial slice: 42 divided by 130 gives 0.32. Above 0.3 counts as ventriculomegaly, and this patient clears it. The trap is treating that as a diagnosis. Evans is a screening measure only: it rises with atrophy as readily as with hydrocephalus, it drifts with the slice you choose and with head shape, and it is deliberately crude. What separates idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus from ex vacuo dilatation is the disproportion around the ventricles: tight crowded sulci at the high convexity and midline, widened Sylvian fissures, and a callosal angle that has closed to an acute value. Report the index, then report those.

quiz.prompt: A 77-year-old with a magnetic gait, urinary urgency and mild inattention. MRI shows enlarged lateral ventricles, crowded tight sulci over the high convexity and at the midline, widened Sylvian fissures, and a callosal angle of 68 degrees measured on a coronal plane at the posterior commissure. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Disproportionate hydrocephalus with an acute callosal angle, a pattern that supports iNPH
choices: Disproportionate hydrocephalus with an acute callosal angle, a pattern that supports iNPH
Ventricular enlargement secondary to generalised atrophy, with sulci widened throughout
Obstruction at the cerebral aqueduct, with a spared fourth ventricle and raised pressure
Chronic small vessel disease with confluent periventricular change accounting for the gait
quiz.explain: This is the DESH pattern: disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus. The point of the word disproportionate is that the cerebrospinal fluid is redistributed rather than uniformly increased, so ventricles and Sylvian fissures enlarge while the sulci at the vertex and along the midline are squeezed shut. The callosal angle, measured on a coronal image perpendicular to the anterior-posterior commissure line at the level of the posterior commissure, falls below about 90 degrees in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, against roughly 100 to 120 degrees in health or in atrophy. Atrophy is excluded here because the convexity sulci are tight, not open. Aqueduct obstruction would enlarge the third ventricle and spare the fourth in a different way and would not crowd the vertex. Small vessel disease often coexists and does not explain the geometry.

quiz.prompt: A referrer asks how you separate the big ventricles of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus from the big ventricles of atrophy. Give the discriminating findings in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: In iNPH the enlargement is disproportionate: the callosal angle is acute at under about 90 degrees, the sulci at the high convexity and midline are tight and crowded, and the Sylvian fissures are widened, whereas atrophy opens the sulci everywhere including the vertex.
quiz.explain: Ventricular size alone cannot make this call, which is why the Evans index disappoints on its own. The discriminators are all about disproportion. A callosal angle below roughly 90 degrees, tight crowded high convexity and medial sulci, and widened Sylvian fissures together form the DESH pattern and are the findings that correlate with shunt response. Atrophy does the opposite: cerebrospinal fluid expands into sulci uniformly, so the vertex is open and the callosal angle stays obtuse. Two extras are worth adding to the report because they move the multidisciplinary decision: focal sulcal dilatation trapped between crowded gyri, which is easily mistaken for atrophy, and any aqueductal flow void that raises the alternative of an obstructive cause. Comorbid small vessel disease should be described rather than used to dismiss the diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old with fluctuating attention, well-formed visual hallucinations and mild parkinsonism. MRI shows relatively preserved hippocampal volumes with mild global atrophy. FDG-PET shows occipital hypometabolism with metabolism in the posterior cingulate preserved relative to the precuneus and cuneus. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Dementia with Lewy bodies, given spared medial temporal lobes and the cingulate island pattern
choices: Dementia with Lewy bodies, given spared medial temporal lobes and the cingulate island pattern
Alzheimer disease, since occipital hypometabolism is the earliest metabolic change it produces
Posterior cortical atrophy, which produces this same occipital and parietal metabolic deficit
Frontotemporal dementia, in which the hippocampi are characteristically preserved on volumetry
quiz.explain: Two features point the same way. Medial temporal structures are relatively spared in dementia with Lewy bodies, which is the opposite of the Alzheimer pattern and is the single most useful structural discriminator on a routine MRI. On FDG-PET the occipital cortex is hypometabolic, and within a hypometabolic posterior belt the posterior cingulate stands out as preserved next to the precuneus and cuneus, the so-called cingulate island. Alzheimer disease does the reverse: it hits the posterior cingulate and precuneus early and typically spares the occipital cortex. Posterior cortical atrophy is visually led but shows marked parieto-occipital atrophy and usually rests on Alzheimer pathology. Frontotemporal dementia shows frontal and anterior temporal loss. If the diagnosis remains uncertain, reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake supports Lewy body disease.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old presents with two years of disinhibition, apathy and loss of empathy, with preserved day-to-day memory. MRI shows asymmetric atrophy of the frontal poles and anterior temporal lobes with knife-edge gyri and widened anterior interhemispheric fissure; the parietal lobes and posterior hippocampi look normal. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, from the asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal loss
choices: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, from the asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal loss
Alzheimer disease, from the precuneus and posterior cingulate volume loss in this distribution
Vascular cognitive impairment, from the confluent deep white matter burden in this distribution
Dementia with Lewy bodies, from the preservation of cortex outside the occipital lobes described
quiz.explain: Frontotemporal degeneration is recognised by where the tissue has gone and by how asymmetric the loss is. Knife-edge gyri at the frontal poles and anterior temporal lobes, a gaping anterior interhemispheric fissure and a widened frontal horn contour on the more affected side are the structural signature, and episodic memory is comparatively preserved because the posterior hippocampus is not the target. Subtypes matter for the report: predominant orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate loss goes with the behavioural variant, severe left anterior temporal loss with semantic variant primary progressive aphasia, and left posterior frontoinsular loss with the non-fluent variant. Alzheimer disease is excluded by the intact parietal and posterior cingulate regions, vascular disease by the absence of a white matter or infarct burden, and Lewy body disease by the frontal, rather than occipital, emphasis.

quiz.prompt: You are setting up MRI surveillance for a patient starting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody. Explain in one or two sentences what the two forms of ARIA look like and which sequence detects each.
quiz.answer: ARIA-E is oedema, seen as gyral swelling with sulcal and parenchymal FLAIR hyperintensity, while ARIA-H is haemorrhage, seen as new microhaemorrhages or superficial siderosis blooming on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or gradient echo.
quiz.explain: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities split cleanly by sequence, so your protocol must carry both. ARIA-E is vasogenic oedema and effusion: FLAIR shows gyral swelling, subcortical white matter hyperintensity and sometimes sulcal hyperintensity, and it is usually parieto-occipital and often multifocal. ARIA-H is blood: new microhaemorrhages and new areas of superficial siderosis that bloom on SWI or T2* gradient echo and are invisible on FLAIR. Read them against the baseline study rather than in isolation, because only incident lesions count. Most ARIA is asymptomatic and detected on scheduled surveillance, but headache, confusion, visual change or seizure in a treated patient is an urgent scan, not a routine one. Report the site, the extent and the count, since severity grading and the decision to pause or stop dosing depend on those numbers.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these regions in the order that neurofibrillary tau pathology, and the atrophy that tracks it, typically involve them in Alzheimer disease.
quiz.answer: transentorhinal-cortex hippocampus temporoparietal-association-cortex primary-visual-cortex
quiz.explain: The Braak scheme describes tau spreading in a stereotyped path, and MRI atrophy follows it a step behind. The earliest stages sit in the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex, which is why the medial temporal atrophy score is the first structural measure to move. Limbic stages then take the hippocampus, amygdala and posterior cingulate, and by this point the amnestic syndrome is usually clinically obvious. Isocortical stages spread into temporoparietal association cortex, giving the precuneus and parietal thinning that anchors an Alzheimer read and drives the posterior atrophy score. Primary sensory and motor cortex, including primary visual cortex, is involved last. Knowing the sequence explains two everyday observations: why an early scan can look normal, and why atypical presentations such as posterior cortical atrophy, which start out of sequence, warrant a different structural search.

quiz.prompt: A patient on an anti-amyloid antibody had 2 microhaemorrhages on the baseline SWI. Surveillance MRI before the fifth infusion shows 9 microhaemorrhages in total. How many incident microhaemorrhages does this represent? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Nine on today's scan minus two that were there at baseline gives seven incident lesions. The arithmetic is trivial and the concept is not: ARIA-H is graded on new lesions counted against the baseline study, never on the running total, so a report that quotes only the total invites either false alarm or false reassurance. On the radiographic severity scale used in the anti-amyloid trials, incident microhaemorrhages are graded mild at four or fewer, moderate at five to nine, and severe at ten or more; new superficial siderosis is scored within ARIA-H as well. Baseline matters in the other direction too, since more than four microhaemorrhages, an area of superficial siderosis or a prior macrohaemorrhage are grounds to withhold treatment under the appropriate use recommendations. Always compare against the same baseline sequence, because SWI finds more lesions than gradient echo.

quiz.prompt: An 86-year-old has a slowly progressive, largely isolated amnestic syndrome. MRI shows medial temporal atrophy scored 4 bilaterally with a strikingly small hippocampus on each side, posterior atrophy 0, and only mild global cortical atrophy. Amyloid PET is negative. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Suspect LATE clinically; MRI does not confirm TDP-43 pathology or hippocampal sclerosis
choices: Suspect LATE clinically; MRI does not confirm TDP-43 pathology or hippocampal sclerosis
Typical Alzheimer disease, in which a negative amyloid scan is the expected result at this age
Frontotemporal dementia, which characteristically opens with isolated hippocampal volume loss
Normal ageing, since hippocampal loss of this degree is anticipated in the ninth decade of life
quiz.explain: A very old patient, a syndrome that stays amnestic, hippocampal atrophy out of all proportion to the rest of the brain, and a negative amyloid scan support suspected limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE). The 2025 clinical criteria may support probable LATE when all clinical requirements are met; MRI and amyloid PET do not demonstrate TDP-43 deposits or confirm hippocampal sclerosis. It is common above 80 and is regularly misreported as Alzheimer disease, which matters now that treatment decisions hinge on amyloid status. Alzheimer disease would be expected to spread beyond the limbic system to the precuneus and parietal cortex and to be amyloid positive; a negative scan in a typical clinical picture argues against it rather than being expected. Frontotemporal degeneration begins frontally and anteriorly in the temporal lobe. And a score of 4 is well beyond the age-adjusted threshold of 3 that applies from 75 onwards, so this is not simple ageing.

quiz.prompt: A physician asks you what a positive amyloid PET actually establishes in a patient with cognitive decline. Answer in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: A positive scan shows tracer binding in cortical grey matter with loss of the normal grey and white matter contrast; it establishes that amyloid pathology is present but does not on its own prove that amyloid is the cause of the patient's cognitive syndrome.
quiz.explain: Amyloid tracers such as florbetapir, flutemetamol and florbetaben bind fibrillar plaque in cortical grey matter. A negative scan keeps white matter tracts bright against a dark cortical ribbon, so the grey and white matter boundary stays sharp; a positive scan fills the cortex, blurring or reversing that contrast. The read is essentially binary, and it is a pathology test, not a syndrome test. Amyloid is present in a substantial minority of cognitively normal older people, so a positive scan in a patient whose picture fits frontotemporal or Lewy body disease may be an incidental finding. Tau PET is the more topographical study, tracking a Braak-like distribution that correlates better with symptoms and atrophy. In current practice the biggest use of amyloid status is gatekeeping anti-amyloid therapy and the surveillance that comes with it.

quiz.prompt: An 82-year-old with a subjective memory complaint and normal formal cognitive testing is scanned. Global cortical atrophy scores 1, medial temporal atrophy scores 2 bilaterally and posterior atrophy scores 0, with no infarcts and only punctate white matter foci. What should your report say?
quiz.answer: Atrophy within the range expected at 82; report it as such and avoid implying degenerative disease
choices: Atrophy within the range expected at 82; report it as such and avoid implying degenerative disease
Atrophy beyond the range expected at 82; report a pattern that is consistent with Alzheimer disease
Atrophy chiefly posterior; report a parietal-predominant pattern and recommend amyloid imaging next
Atrophy chiefly frontal; report a frontotemporal pattern and recommend neuropsychological assessment
quiz.explain: This is the commonest way a structured read goes wrong. Every visual scale is age-dependent, and the thresholds move upward with each decade. For medial temporal atrophy the widely applied cut-off is 2 or more below 75 but 3 or more at 75 and above, so a score of 2 in an 82-year-old is unremarkable. Global cortical atrophy runs 0 to 3 and a score of 1 is mild and expected here. Posterior atrophy runs 0 to 3, and it is 0. The other options misdescribe the measurements: nothing posterior or frontal predominates. Writing that the appearances are within the expected range for the age is a positive finding, not a failure to commit, and it protects a worried patient from a diagnosis the images do not support. Note the burden and offer follow-up if the clinical picture changes.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with two years of progressive episodic memory loss. On coronal T1 angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, the choroid fissures are widened, the temporal horns enlarged and the hippocampal height reduced, giving a medial temporal atrophy score of 2 on each side. Posterior atrophy is 0 and the frontal lobes look normal. What do you report?
quiz.answer: Medial temporal atrophy beyond the age cut-off, a pattern that supports Alzheimer disease
choices: Medial temporal atrophy beyond the age cut-off, a pattern that supports Alzheimer disease
Medial temporal atrophy still within the expected range at this age, so a normal study
Global cortical atrophy out of proportion to the rest, favouring a vascular contribution
Posterior-predominant atrophy out of keeping with the age, favouring a parietal syndrome
quiz.explain: The Scheltens medial temporal atrophy (MTA) scale runs 0 to 4 and is read on a coronal T1 angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, weighing three things together: width of the choroid fissure, width of the temporal horn, and height of the hippocampal formation. The score only means something once you attach an age. The cut-off in common use is a score of 2 or more below the age of 75, and 3 or more at 75 and above; scoring without that adjustment is how normal ageing gets reported as disease. At 68 with a score of 2 bilaterally this study sits above the threshold, and in an amnestic presentation that supports Alzheimer disease. The other readings do not fit what was measured: global cortical atrophy and frontal change were not present, and the posterior atrophy score was 0.

quiz.prompt: On an axial CT slice through the frontal horns, the maximal width across the frontal horns is 42 mm and the maximal internal diameter of the skull on the same slice is 130 mm. Calculate the Evans index. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The Evans index is the maximal width across the frontal horns divided by the maximal internal diameter of the inner table on the same axial slice: 42 divided by 130 gives 0.32. Above 0.3 counts as ventriculomegaly, and this patient clears it. The trap is treating that as a diagnosis. Evans is a screening measure only: it rises with atrophy as readily as with hydrocephalus, it drifts with the slice you choose and with head shape, and it is deliberately crude. What separates idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus from ex vacuo dilatation is the disproportion around the ventricles: tight crowded sulci at the high convexity and midline, widened Sylvian fissures, and a callosal angle that has closed to an acute value. Report the index, then report those.

quiz.prompt: A 77-year-old with a magnetic gait, urinary urgency and mild inattention. MRI shows enlarged lateral ventricles, crowded tight sulci over the high convexity and at the midline, widened Sylvian fissures, and a callosal angle of 68 degrees measured on a coronal plane at the posterior commissure. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Disproportionate hydrocephalus with an acute callosal angle, a pattern that supports iNPH
choices: Disproportionate hydrocephalus with an acute callosal angle, a pattern that supports iNPH
Ventricular enlargement secondary to generalised atrophy, with sulci widened throughout
Obstruction at the cerebral aqueduct, with a spared fourth ventricle and raised pressure
Chronic small vessel disease with confluent periventricular change accounting for the gait
quiz.explain: This is the DESH pattern: disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus. The point of the word disproportionate is that the cerebrospinal fluid is redistributed rather than uniformly increased, so ventricles and Sylvian fissures enlarge while the sulci at the vertex and along the midline are squeezed shut. The callosal angle, measured on a coronal image perpendicular to the anterior-posterior commissure line at the level of the posterior commissure, falls below about 90 degrees in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, against roughly 100 to 120 degrees in health or in atrophy. Atrophy is excluded here because the convexity sulci are tight, not open. Aqueduct obstruction would enlarge the third ventricle and spare the fourth in a different way and would not crowd the vertex. Small vessel disease often coexists and does not explain the geometry.

quiz.prompt: A referrer asks how you separate the big ventricles of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus from the big ventricles of atrophy. Give the discriminating findings in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: In iNPH the enlargement is disproportionate: the callosal angle is acute at under about 90 degrees, the sulci at the high convexity and midline are tight and crowded, and the Sylvian fissures are widened, whereas atrophy opens the sulci everywhere including the vertex.
quiz.explain: Ventricular size alone cannot make this call, which is why the Evans index disappoints on its own. The discriminators are all about disproportion. A callosal angle below roughly 90 degrees, tight crowded high convexity and medial sulci, and widened Sylvian fissures together form the DESH pattern and are the findings that correlate with shunt response. Atrophy does the opposite: cerebrospinal fluid expands into sulci uniformly, so the vertex is open and the callosal angle stays obtuse. Two extras are worth adding to the report because they move the multidisciplinary decision: focal sulcal dilatation trapped between crowded gyri, which is easily mistaken for atrophy, and any aqueductal flow void that raises the alternative of an obstructive cause. Comorbid small vessel disease should be described rather than used to dismiss the diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old with fluctuating attention, well-formed visual hallucinations and mild parkinsonism. MRI shows relatively preserved hippocampal volumes with mild global atrophy. FDG-PET shows occipital hypometabolism with metabolism in the posterior cingulate preserved relative to the precuneus and cuneus. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Dementia with Lewy bodies, given spared medial temporal lobes and the cingulate island pattern
choices: Dementia with Lewy bodies, given spared medial temporal lobes and the cingulate island pattern
Alzheimer disease, since occipital hypometabolism is the earliest metabolic change it produces
Posterior cortical atrophy, which produces this same occipital and parietal metabolic deficit
Frontotemporal dementia, in which the hippocampi are characteristically preserved on volumetry
quiz.explain: Two features point the same way. Medial temporal structures are relatively spared in dementia with Lewy bodies, which is the opposite of the Alzheimer pattern and is the single most useful structural discriminator on a routine MRI. On FDG-PET the occipital cortex is hypometabolic, and within a hypometabolic posterior belt the posterior cingulate stands out as preserved next to the precuneus and cuneus, the so-called cingulate island. Alzheimer disease does the reverse: it hits the posterior cingulate and precuneus early and typically spares the occipital cortex. Posterior cortical atrophy is visually led but shows marked parieto-occipital atrophy and usually rests on Alzheimer pathology. Frontotemporal dementia shows frontal and anterior temporal loss. If the diagnosis remains uncertain, reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake supports Lewy body disease.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old presents with two years of disinhibition, apathy and loss of empathy, with preserved day-to-day memory. MRI shows asymmetric atrophy of the frontal poles and anterior temporal lobes with knife-edge gyri and widened anterior interhemispheric fissure; the parietal lobes and posterior hippocampi look normal. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, from the asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal loss
choices: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, from the asymmetric frontal and anterior temporal loss
Alzheimer disease, from the precuneus and posterior cingulate volume loss in this distribution
Vascular cognitive impairment, from the confluent deep white matter burden in this distribution
Dementia with Lewy bodies, from the preservation of cortex outside the occipital lobes described
quiz.explain: Frontotemporal degeneration is recognised by where the tissue has gone and by how asymmetric the loss is. Knife-edge gyri at the frontal poles and anterior temporal lobes, a gaping anterior interhemispheric fissure and a widened frontal horn contour on the more affected side are the structural signature, and episodic memory is comparatively preserved because the posterior hippocampus is not the target. Subtypes matter for the report: predominant orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate loss goes with the behavioural variant, severe left anterior temporal loss with semantic variant primary progressive aphasia, and left posterior frontoinsular loss with the non-fluent variant. Alzheimer disease is excluded by the intact parietal and posterior cingulate regions, vascular disease by the absence of a white matter or infarct burden, and Lewy body disease by the frontal, rather than occipital, emphasis.

quiz.prompt: You are setting up MRI surveillance for a patient starting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody. Explain in one or two sentences what the two forms of ARIA look like and which sequence detects each.
quiz.answer: ARIA-E is oedema, seen as gyral swelling with sulcal and parenchymal FLAIR hyperintensity, while ARIA-H is haemorrhage, seen as new microhaemorrhages or superficial siderosis blooming on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or gradient echo.
quiz.explain: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities split cleanly by sequence, so your protocol must carry both. ARIA-E is vasogenic oedema and effusion: FLAIR shows gyral swelling, subcortical white matter hyperintensity and sometimes sulcal hyperintensity, and it is usually parieto-occipital and often multifocal. ARIA-H is blood: new microhaemorrhages and new areas of superficial siderosis that bloom on SWI or T2* gradient echo and are invisible on FLAIR. Read them against the baseline study rather than in isolation, because only incident lesions count. Most ARIA is asymptomatic and detected on scheduled surveillance, but headache, confusion, visual change or seizure in a treated patient is an urgent scan, not a routine one. Report the site, the extent and the count, since severity grading and the decision to pause or stop dosing depend on those numbers.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these regions in the order that neurofibrillary tau pathology, and the atrophy that tracks it, typically involve them in Alzheimer disease.
quiz.answer: transentorhinal-cortex hippocampus temporoparietal-association-cortex primary-visual-cortex
quiz.explain: The Braak scheme describes tau spreading in a stereotyped path, and MRI atrophy follows it a step behind. The earliest stages sit in the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex, which is why the medial temporal atrophy score is the first structural measure to move. Limbic stages then take the hippocampus, amygdala and posterior cingulate, and by this point the amnestic syndrome is usually clinically obvious. Isocortical stages spread into temporoparietal association cortex, giving the precuneus and parietal thinning that anchors an Alzheimer read and drives the posterior atrophy score. Primary sensory and motor cortex, including primary visual cortex, is involved last. Knowing the sequence explains two everyday observations: why an early scan can look normal, and why atypical presentations such as posterior cortical atrophy, which start out of sequence, warrant a different structural search.

quiz.prompt: A patient on an anti-amyloid antibody had 2 microhaemorrhages on the baseline SWI. Surveillance MRI before the fifth infusion shows 9 microhaemorrhages in total. How many incident microhaemorrhages does this represent? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Nine on today's scan minus two that were there at baseline gives seven incident lesions. The arithmetic is trivial and the concept is not: ARIA-H is graded on new lesions counted against the baseline study, never on the running total, so a report that quotes only the total invites either false alarm or false reassurance. On the radiographic severity scale used in the anti-amyloid trials, incident microhaemorrhages are graded mild at four or fewer, moderate at five to nine, and severe at ten or more; new superficial siderosis is scored within ARIA-H as well. Baseline matters in the other direction too, since more than four microhaemorrhages, an area of superficial siderosis or a prior macrohaemorrhage are grounds to withhold treatment under the appropriate use recommendations. Always compare against the same baseline sequence, because SWI finds more lesions than gradient echo.

quiz.prompt: An 86-year-old has a slowly progressive, largely isolated amnestic syndrome. MRI shows medial temporal atrophy scored 4 bilaterally with a strikingly small hippocampus on each side, posterior atrophy 0, and only mild global cortical atrophy. Amyloid PET is negative. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Suspect LATE clinically; MRI does not confirm TDP-43 pathology or hippocampal sclerosis
choices: Suspect LATE clinically; MRI does not confirm TDP-43 pathology or hippocampal sclerosis
Typical Alzheimer disease, in which a negative amyloid scan is the expected result at this age
Frontotemporal dementia, which characteristically opens with isolated hippocampal volume loss
Normal ageing, since hippocampal loss of this degree is anticipated in the ninth decade of life
quiz.explain: A very old patient, a syndrome that stays amnestic, hippocampal atrophy out of all proportion to the rest of the brain, and a negative amyloid scan support suspected limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE). The 2025 clinical criteria may support probable LATE when all clinical requirements are met; MRI and amyloid PET do not demonstrate TDP-43 deposits or confirm hippocampal sclerosis. It is common above 80 and is regularly misreported as Alzheimer disease, which matters now that treatment decisions hinge on amyloid status. Alzheimer disease would be expected to spread beyond the limbic system to the precuneus and parietal cortex and to be amyloid positive; a negative scan in a typical clinical picture argues against it rather than being expected. Frontotemporal degeneration begins frontally and anteriorly in the temporal lobe. And a score of 4 is well beyond the age-adjusted threshold of 3 that applies from 75 onwards, so this is not simple ageing.

quiz.prompt: A physician asks you what a positive amyloid PET actually establishes in a patient with cognitive decline. Answer in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: A positive scan shows tracer binding in cortical grey matter with loss of the normal grey and white matter contrast; it establishes that amyloid pathology is present but does not on its own prove that amyloid is the cause of the patient's cognitive syndrome.
quiz.explain: Amyloid tracers such as florbetapir, flutemetamol and florbetaben bind fibrillar plaque in cortical grey matter. A negative scan keeps white matter tracts bright against a dark cortical ribbon, so the grey and white matter boundary stays sharp; a positive scan fills the cortex, blurring or reversing that contrast. The read is essentially binary, and it is a pathology test, not a syndrome test. Amyloid is present in a substantial minority of cognitively normal older people, so a positive scan in a patient whose picture fits frontotemporal or Lewy body disease may be an incidental finding. Tau PET is the more topographical study, tracking a Braak-like distribution that correlates better with symptoms and atrophy. In current practice the biggest use of amyloid status is gatekeeping anti-amyloid therapy and the surveillance that comes with it.

quiz.prompt: An 82-year-old with a subjective memory complaint and normal formal cognitive testing is scanned. Global cortical atrophy scores 1, medial temporal atrophy scores 2 bilaterally and posterior atrophy scores 0, with no infarcts and only punctate white matter foci. What should your report say?
quiz.answer: Atrophy within the range expected at 82; report it as such and avoid implying degenerative disease
choices: Atrophy within the range expected at 82; report it as such and avoid implying degenerative disease
Atrophy beyond the range expected at 82; report a pattern that is consistent with Alzheimer disease
Atrophy chiefly posterior; report a parietal-predominant pattern and recommend amyloid imaging next
Atrophy chiefly frontal; report a frontotemporal pattern and recommend neuropsychological assessment
quiz.explain: This is the commonest way a structured read goes wrong. Every visual scale is age-dependent, and the thresholds move upward with each decade. For medial temporal atrophy the widely applied cut-off is 2 or more below 75 but 3 or more at 75 and above, so a score of 2 in an 82-year-old is unremarkable. Global cortical atrophy runs 0 to 3 and a score of 1 is mild and expected here. Posterior atrophy runs 0 to 3, and it is 0. The other options misdescribe the measurements: nothing posterior or frontal predominates. Writing that the appearances are within the expected range for the age is a positive finding, not a failure to commit, and it protects a worried patient from a diagnosis the images do not support. Note the burden and offer follow-up if the clinical picture changes.

approach.step: Run a dedicated epilepsy protocol, not a routine brain
approach.detail: T1 for cortical thickness and the grey-white interface, FLAIR for cortical and subcortical hyperintensity, T2* or SWI for haemoglobin breakdown products.
Compare the two on coronal images: volume, internal architecture and signal. Mesial temporal sclerosis is the commonest surgically remediable lesion.
Look for blurring of the grey-white interface, abnormal cortical thickness and the transmantle sign of focal cortical dysplasia.

approach.step: Look for grey matter where it should not be
approach.detail: Subependymal and subcortical heterotopia, and the abnormal gyral pattern of polymicrogyria.

approach.step: Check for a cortical tumour or cavernoma
approach.detail: DNET and ganglioglioma sit in the cortex; a cavernoma shows on T2* or SWI when it is invisible elsewhere.

pitfalls: Accepting a routine brain MRI as a negative epilepsy study. Without the dedicated sequences the lesion is simply not resolvable.
Reading the hippocampi on axial images alone. The comparison that shows sclerosis is on coronal slices, side by side.
Omitting T2* or SWI. A cavernoma may be the whole answer and it can be invisible on T1 and FLAIR.
Missing focal cortical dysplasia because you looked for a mass. The findings are blurring of the grey-white interface, abnormal cortical thickness and the transmantle sign.
Calling subependymal heterotopia a lesion of the ventricle wall. It is normal grey matter in the wrong place, and it follows cortex on every sequence.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old with drug-resistant focal seizures is referred to a surgical programme. The only imaging is a 1.5T study with 5 mm axial T2 and FLAIR and 5 mm axial T1, reported as normal two years ago. What do you arrange?
quiz.answer: Rescan at 3T with millimetric 3D T1 and FLAIR plus a high-resolution coronal T2 through the hippocampi
choices: Rescan at 3T with millimetric 3D T1 and FLAIR plus a high-resolution coronal T2 through the hippocampi
Repeat the same axial protocol with gadolinium, since epileptogenic lesions enhance once they are mature
Add diffusion and perfusion to the same axial protocol, which will expose the abnormal cortical region
Move directly to intracranial electrodes, since a study reported as normal ends the structural work-up
quiz.explain: A routine brain MRI is built to exclude a mass or a bleed, and it is the wrong instrument for this question. Thick axial slices partial-volume the cortical ribbon, so the blurred grey and white matter junction of a dysplasia is averaged away, and an axial plane cuts the hippocampus obliquely so that mild volume loss and signal change go unseen. The HARNESS-MRI protocol from the ILAE neuroimaging task force fixes exactly this: millimetric isotropic 3D T1, millimetric isotropic 3D FLAIR, and a two-dimensional coronal T2 with submillimetric in-plane resolution angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, preferably at 3T. Contrast adds almost nothing to a first-pass epilepsy protocol because the common lesions do not enhance. Diffusion and perfusion do not resolve the cortical ribbon. And a negative outside study is a reason to rescan properly, not to abandon imaging.

quiz.prompt: A routine two-dimensional FLAIR is acquired at 1.0 mm by 1.0 mm in-plane with 5 mm slices. The 3D FLAIR of an epilepsy protocol is 1.0 mm isotropic. By what factor is the voxel volume of the routine sequence larger? Answer as a number to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The routine voxel is 1.0 by 1.0 by 5.0, which is 5 cubic millimetres; the isotropic voxel is 1 cubic millimetre. The ratio is 5.0. That single figure explains most missed lesions in epilepsy. Signal in a voxel is the average of everything inside it, so a 5 mm slice through the cortex blends grey matter, white matter and cerebrospinal fluid and quietly erases the two findings that matter most: subtle blurring of the grey and white matter junction, and a thin band of high FLAIR signal running toward the ventricle. Isotropic voxels also let you reformat in any plane from one acquisition, so an abnormality suspected on the axial reconstruction can be confirmed on coronal and sagittal reformats of the same data rather than requiring the patient back.

quiz.prompt: A radiographer asks you to specify the three core sequences of the HARNESS-MRI epilepsy protocol. Describe them in one or two sentences, including the geometry that matters.
quiz.answer: A millimetric isotropic 3D T1, a millimetric isotropic 3D FLAIR, and a high in-plane resolution coronal T2 angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, acquired at 3 tesla wherever possible.
quiz.explain: HARNESS-MRI, the harmonised structural protocol proposed by the ILAE neuroimaging task force, was designed to be short enough that any department can run it. The isotropic 3D T1 gives the cortical ribbon and supports post-processing and surface analysis. The isotropic 3D FLAIR carries the signal abnormality of dysplasia and hippocampal sclerosis and reformats freely. The two-dimensional coronal T2, with in-plane resolution well below a millimetre and angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, is what lets you judge hippocampal size, signal and internal architecture side by side. A susceptibility-weighted or gradient echo sequence is a sensible addition for blood products when a cavernoma is in question. Contrast is not part of the core protocol, and adding it before a proper structural study is a common way to waste a scan slot.

quiz.prompt: A coronal T2 shows a small right hippocampus with increased FLAIR signal and loss of the normal internal digitations, and the right temporal horn is dilated. Which additional finding on the same study would most support the diagnosis you are considering?
quiz.answer: Atrophy of the ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body with a small ipsilateral temporal lobe
choices: Atrophy of the ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body with a small ipsilateral temporal lobe
Avid nodular enhancement of the hippocampal head after gadolinium with surrounding oedema
Restricted diffusion throughout the hippocampal body persisting on the apparent diffusion map
Enlargement of the contralateral hippocampus with high signal in its adjacent white matter
quiz.explain: Hippocampal sclerosis is read on three primary features: reduced volume, raised T2 and FLAIR signal, and loss of the internal architecture, meaning the digitations of the head and the internal striations blur into a featureless block. Because the circuit degenerates as a whole, the supporting findings sit downstream: the ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body atrophy, the temporal horn dilates to fill the space, the collateral white matter loses its grey-to-white distinction, and the whole temporal lobe may be slightly small. Those extras are what convert a suspicion into a confident lateralisation, and lateralisation is the whole point in a surgical candidate. Avid enhancement with oedema should redirect you to a tumour or encephalitis. Persistent restricted diffusion suggests a recent insult, not chronic sclerosis. A big contralateral hippocampus is not a recognised sign and risks lateralising to the wrong side.

quiz.prompt: Describe the transmantle sign in one or two sentences, and say what its presence tells you about the underlying lesion.
quiz.answer: It is a funnel-shaped band of T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity tapering from thickened, blurred cortex down to the ventricular surface, and it indicates a focal cortical dysplasia, characteristically the ILAE type IIb form with balloon cells.
quiz.explain: The sign traces the path abnormal cells took during radial migration, so it runs the full thickness of the mantle from the cortical surface to the ventricular ependyma, widest at the cortex and narrowing as it descends. On isotropic 3D FLAIR it is often the only unequivocal abnormality, which is why that sequence is a protocol core. Look for its companions in the same place: cortical thickening, blurring of the grey and white matter junction, an abnormal sulcal or gyral configuration, and sometimes a deep unusually oriented sulcus at the epicentre. Its value is practical rather than descriptive. A transmantle sign identifies a discrete, resectable target with a good chance of seizure freedom, and it turns an MRI-negative patient into an MRI-positive one, which changes both the surgical decision and the odds quoted to the patient.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old has had focal seizures with impaired awareness since childhood. MRI shows a cortically based, multicystic bubbly lesion in the left temporal lobe with a bright FLAIR rim, no surrounding oedema, no enhancement, and gentle scalloping of the inner table of the skull. What is the lesion and how should the report frame it?
quiz.answer: A DNET, framed as a long-standing epileptogenic cortical lesion rather than an aggressive tumour
choices: A DNET, framed as a long-standing epileptogenic cortical lesion rather than an aggressive tumour
A ganglioglioma, framed around the enhancing mural nodule and calcification that characterise it
A cavernoma, framed around the complete haemosiderin rim and the blooming seen on susceptibility
An acute infarct, framed around the cortical swelling and restricted diffusion in a vascular territory
quiz.explain: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumours are cortically based, wedge-shaped or bubbly on T2, and characteristically have a bright FLAIR rim around a cluster of microcysts. They cause no oedema and little mass effect, and the slow remodelling of the overlying inner table testifies to how long they have been there. Enhancement is usually absent or faint. The reporting framing matters as much as the label: this is a lesion whose significance is seizures, so the report should support a planned epilepsy surgery pathway rather than trigger an urgent oncological work-up. A ganglioglioma, the other classic long-standing temporal lesion, more often shows a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule and calcification. A cavernoma would show a complete haemosiderin rim with marked blooming. An infarct would be territorial, swollen and diffusion-restricted, and would not scallop bone.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old with focal seizures has MRI showing smooth ovoid nodules lining both lateral ventricles. The nodules follow grey matter signal exactly on T1, T2 and FLAIR, do not enhance, and show no blooming on susceptibility imaging. What do you conclude and advise?
quiz.answer: Periventricular nodular heterotopia: grey matter in the wrong place, so no biopsy is needed
choices: Periventricular nodular heterotopia: grey matter in the wrong place, so no biopsy is needed
Subependymal nodules of tuberous sclerosis: look for calcification and cortical tubers as well
Subependymal tumour spread: the nodules would enhance and follow cerebrospinal fluid pathways
Old subependymal haemorrhage: blood products lining the ependymal surface after a preterm bleed
quiz.explain: The discriminator is signal, and the rule is simple: heterotopic grey matter is grey matter, so it matches cortex on every sequence, does not enhance, and does not bloom. Subependymal nodules in tuberous sclerosis often calcify and bloom, frequently enhance, and travel with cortical tubers and radial migration lines. Metastatic or lymphomatous subependymal deposits enhance and are usually irregular. Old germinal matrix haemorrhage leaves susceptibility-positive residue. Once heterotopia is established the useful work begins: describe how extensive and how symmetric the nodules are, look for the associated cortical malformation and for a thin corpus callosum or cerebellar hypoplasia, and mention that bilateral diffuse periventricular nodular heterotopia is associated with FLNA variants, since that carries implications for the patient's family as well as for surgical planning.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these investigations in the order a presurgical epilepsy programme would usually deploy them for a patient whose first MRI was reported as normal.
quiz.answer: HARNESS-MRI morphometric-post-processing FDG-PET ictal-SPECT intracranial-EEG
quiz.explain: The ladder climbs from cheap and non-invasive toward expensive and invasive, and each rung is only worth attempting once the one below it has been done properly. First repeat the structural study with a dedicated protocol, because a large share of so-called MRI-negative patients simply had the wrong sequences. Then run morphometric post-processing on the isotropic 3D T1, comparing junction and thickness maps against a normal database to flag candidate regions for a targeted re-read. Interictal FDG-PET follows, showing regional hypometabolism that usually extends beyond the lesion but reliably lateralises. Ictal SPECT, ideally coregistered with MRI, requires an injection during a seizure and is therefore resource-heavy and reserved for continuing uncertainty. Intracranial EEG sits at the top: it defines the seizure onset zone directly but carries surgical risk, and it needs a hypothesis to sample, which is precisely what every earlier rung supplies.

quiz.prompt: You are planning the dedicated coronal T2 stack. The hippocampus measures 4.0 cm along its long axis and you will use 2 mm slices with no interslice gap. How many slices are needed to cover it end to end? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Forty millimetres of coverage divided by 2 mm per contiguous slice gives 20 slices, and in practice you would prescribe a few more at each end so that the head and tail are not clipped. The planning point behind the arithmetic is that this stack must be angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, prescribed on a sagittal or oblique reformat, and must run from in front of the hippocampal head to behind the tail. Coverage failures are a real cause of missed sclerosis, because the head is where the digitations live and the tail is where subtle atrophy declares itself. Thin contiguous slices also preserve the side-to-side comparison that the coronal plane exists to provide: symmetry is judged by looking at both hippocampi in the same slice, which an oblique or gapped acquisition quietly destroys.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old with focal seizures has a 12 mm lesion at the right frontal grey and white matter junction with a mixed-signal popcorn core and a complete dark rim on T2, blooming on gradient echo, with no oedema. A cousin had seizures and a brain haemorrhage. What do you add to the study and why?
quiz.answer: Whole-brain susceptibility-weighted imaging, to search for the additional lesions of the familial form
choices: Whole-brain susceptibility-weighted imaging, to search for the additional lesions of the familial form
Perfusion imaging through the lesion, to separate a cavernoma from a haemorrhagic metastatic deposit
Spectroscopy through the lesion, to demonstrate the choline elevation of a vascular malformation
Early and delayed contrast imaging, to demonstrate the rapid arteriovenous shunting that it contains
quiz.explain: The described lesion is a cavernous malformation: locules of blood of differing ages give the popcorn core, and the complete haemosiderin rim blooms heavily on susceptibility-sensitive sequences. With a family history the question is no longer what the lesion is but how many there are, because multiplicity defines familial cerebral cavernous malformation and changes counselling, surveillance and the genetic conversation for relatives. Susceptibility-weighted imaging is far more sensitive than gradient echo for the tiny punctate lesions that make the diagnosis, so it should cover the whole brain. Perfusion and spectroscopy add nothing to a lesion this characteristic. Cavernomas are angiographically occult and contain no arteriovenous shunt, so dynamic contrast imaging is misdirected, though it is worth looking for an associated developmental venous anomaly, which must be preserved if the cavernoma is resected.

quiz.prompt: Describe how polymicrogyria appears on a millimetric 3D T1 and name the associated finding that often accompanies it.
quiz.answer: The cortical ribbon looks irregular, stippled and overly folded, thin in reality but mimicking thickening at low resolution, most often around the sylvian fissure, and it is frequently accompanied by anomalous draining veins.
quiz.explain: Polymicrogyria is a disorder of late migration and cortical organisation in which many small gyri fuse at the surface. On a thick-slice study the packed miniature gyri average together and the cortical ribbon simply looks thick and lumpy, which is how it gets confused with pachygyria; on millimetric isotropic T1 the true stippled, bumpy inner surface with a shallow irregular sulcal pattern becomes visible. The perisylvian region is the commonest site, and bilateral perisylvian involvement produces a recognisable clinical syndrome with oromotor difficulty. Look for the companions: anomalous or enlarged draining veins over the affected cortex, an overlying arachnoid or subarachnoid space that appears too generous, and underlying white matter volume loss. Distribution matters for aetiology, since a unilateral perisylvian distribution raises congenital cytomegalovirus or an in utero vascular insult.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old with drug-resistant frontal lobe epilepsy has a full HARNESS protocol reported as normal. Scalp EEG and semiology both point to the right frontal lobe. What is the most useful next imaging step?
quiz.answer: Run morphometric post-processing against a normal database, then re-read with that hypothesis
choices: Run morphometric post-processing against a normal database, then re-read with that hypothesis
Report the study as normal and close the structural work-up before the surgical meeting is held
Repeat the identical MRI in twelve months and wait for the abnormality to declare itself over time
Rely on interictal FDG-PET alone and take the hypometabolic lobe as the resection target directly
quiz.explain: Around a quarter to a third of drug-resistant focal epilepsies are called MRI-negative, and a good share of those are really reader-negative: the lesion is on the images but is too subtle for an unguided read. Morphometric post-processing helps twice over. It builds junction, extension and thickness maps from the isotropic 3D T1 and compares them voxel by voxel against a normal cohort, generating candidate regions; and it then licenses a targeted second read, where a radiologist looks at one gyrus with the electroclinical hypothesis in hand. That combination converts a meaningful number of negative studies into positive ones, and finding the lesion improves the odds of seizure freedom after surgery. Simply repeating the same scan later rarely helps in an adult. FDG-PET is valuable but its hypometabolism is regional and typically wider than the lesion, so it lateralises rather than defines a resection margin.

module_contract.goal: Design and read a dedicated epilepsy MRI, find the lesions a routine brain study hides, and know what to do next when the protocol comes back negative.

approach.step: Run a dedicated epilepsy protocol, not a routine brain
approach.detail: Use millimetric isotropic 3D T1 for morphology, millimetric isotropic 3D FLAIR for signal, and high-resolution coronal T2 perpendicular to the hippocampal long axes for hippocampal internal architecture. Add susceptibility and other sequences for the clinical question.
Compare the two on coronal images: volume, internal architecture and signal. Mesial temporal sclerosis is the commonest surgically remediable lesion.
Look for blurring of the grey-white interface, abnormal cortical thickness and the transmantle sign of focal cortical dysplasia.

approach.step: Look for grey matter where it should not be
approach.detail: Subependymal and subcortical heterotopia, and the abnormal gyral pattern of polymicrogyria.

approach.step: Check for a cortical tumour or cavernoma
approach.detail: DNET and ganglioglioma sit in the cortex; a cavernoma shows on T2* or SWI when it is invisible elsewhere.

pitfalls: Accepting a routine brain MRI as a negative epilepsy study. Without the dedicated sequences the lesion is simply not resolvable.
Reading the hippocampi on axial images alone. The comparison that shows sclerosis is on coronal slices, side by side.
Omitting T2* or SWI. A cavernoma may be the whole answer and it can be invisible on T1 and FLAIR.
Missing focal cortical dysplasia because you looked for a mass. The findings are blurring of the grey-white interface, abnormal cortical thickness and the transmantle sign.
Calling subependymal heterotopia a lesion of the ventricle wall. It is normal grey matter in the wrong place, and it follows cortex on every sequence.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old with drug-resistant focal seizures is referred to a surgical programme. The only imaging is a 1.5T study with 5 mm axial T2 and FLAIR and 5 mm axial T1, reported as normal two years ago. What do you arrange?
quiz.answer: Rescan at 3T with millimetric 3D T1 and FLAIR plus a high-resolution coronal T2 through the hippocampi
choices: Rescan at 3T with millimetric 3D T1 and FLAIR plus a high-resolution coronal T2 through the hippocampi
Repeat the same axial protocol with gadolinium, since epileptogenic lesions enhance once they are mature
Add diffusion and perfusion to the same axial protocol, which will expose the abnormal cortical region
Move directly to intracranial electrodes, since a study reported as normal ends the structural work-up
quiz.explain: A routine brain MRI is built to exclude a mass or a bleed, and it is the wrong instrument for this question. Thick axial slices partial-volume the cortical ribbon, so the blurred grey and white matter junction of a dysplasia is averaged away, and an axial plane cuts the hippocampus obliquely so that mild volume loss and signal change go unseen. The HARNESS-MRI protocol from the ILAE neuroimaging task force fixes exactly this: millimetric isotropic 3D T1, millimetric isotropic 3D FLAIR, and a two-dimensional coronal T2 with submillimetric in-plane resolution angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, preferably at 3T. Contrast adds almost nothing to a first-pass epilepsy protocol because the common lesions do not enhance. Diffusion and perfusion do not resolve the cortical ribbon. And a negative outside study is a reason to rescan properly, not to abandon imaging.

quiz.prompt: A routine two-dimensional FLAIR is acquired at 1.0 mm by 1.0 mm in-plane with 5 mm slices. The 3D FLAIR of an epilepsy protocol is 1.0 mm isotropic. By what factor is the voxel volume of the routine sequence larger? Answer as a number to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The routine voxel is 1.0 by 1.0 by 5.0, which is 5 cubic millimetres; the isotropic voxel is 1 cubic millimetre. The ratio is 5.0. That single figure explains most missed lesions in epilepsy. Signal in a voxel is the average of everything inside it, so a 5 mm slice through the cortex blends grey matter, white matter and cerebrospinal fluid and quietly erases the two findings that matter most: subtle blurring of the grey and white matter junction, and a thin band of high FLAIR signal running toward the ventricle. Isotropic voxels also let you reformat in any plane from one acquisition, so an abnormality suspected on the axial reconstruction can be confirmed on coronal and sagittal reformats of the same data rather than requiring the patient back.

quiz.prompt: A radiographer asks you to specify the three core sequences of the HARNESS-MRI epilepsy protocol. Describe them in one or two sentences, including the geometry that matters.
quiz.answer: A millimetric isotropic 3D T1, a millimetric isotropic 3D FLAIR, and a high in-plane resolution coronal T2 angled perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, acquired at 3 tesla wherever possible.
quiz.explain: HARNESS-MRI, the harmonised structural protocol proposed by the ILAE neuroimaging task force, was designed to be short enough that any department can run it. The isotropic 3D T1 gives the cortical ribbon and supports post-processing and surface analysis. The isotropic 3D FLAIR carries the signal abnormality of dysplasia and hippocampal sclerosis and reformats freely. The two-dimensional coronal T2, with in-plane resolution well below a millimetre and angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, is what lets you judge hippocampal size, signal and internal architecture side by side. A susceptibility-weighted or gradient echo sequence is a sensible addition for blood products when a cavernoma is in question. Contrast is not part of the core protocol, and adding it before a proper structural study is a common way to waste a scan slot.

quiz.prompt: A coronal T2 shows a small right hippocampus with increased FLAIR signal and loss of the normal internal digitations, and the right temporal horn is dilated. Which additional finding on the same study would most support the diagnosis you are considering?
quiz.answer: Atrophy of the ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body with a small ipsilateral temporal lobe
choices: Atrophy of the ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body with a small ipsilateral temporal lobe
Avid nodular enhancement of the hippocampal head after gadolinium with surrounding oedema
Restricted diffusion throughout the hippocampal body persisting on the apparent diffusion map
Enlargement of the contralateral hippocampus with high signal in its adjacent white matter
quiz.explain: Hippocampal sclerosis is read on three primary features: reduced volume, raised T2 and FLAIR signal, and loss of the internal architecture, meaning the digitations of the head and the internal striations blur into a featureless block. Because the circuit degenerates as a whole, the supporting findings sit downstream: the ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body atrophy, the temporal horn dilates to fill the space, the collateral white matter loses its grey-to-white distinction, and the whole temporal lobe may be slightly small. Those extras are what convert a suspicion into a confident lateralisation, and lateralisation is the whole point in a surgical candidate. Avid enhancement with oedema should redirect you to a tumour or encephalitis. Persistent restricted diffusion suggests a recent insult, not chronic sclerosis. A big contralateral hippocampus is not a recognised sign and risks lateralising to the wrong side.

quiz.prompt: Describe the transmantle sign in one or two sentences, and say what its presence tells you about the underlying lesion.
quiz.answer: A funnel-shaped band of T2/FLAIR hyperintensity extends from abnormal cortex towards the ventricular surface. It supports focal cortical dysplasia type II, most often IIb, but MRI does not demonstrate balloon cells or establish the histological subtype.
quiz.explain: Follow the subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensity towards the ventricular surface and inspect the corresponding cortex on high-resolution T1. Assess cortical thickness, the grey-white junction and sulcogyral morphology in the same location. The transmantle pattern supports FCD type II, most often IIb, but does not demonstrate balloon cells or establish a histopathological subtype. Describe the lesion location and extent and relate them to the supplied electroclinical findings. Presurgical decisions require the full epilepsy evaluation.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old has had focal seizures with impaired awareness since childhood. MRI shows a cortically based, multicystic bubbly lesion in the left temporal lobe with a bright FLAIR rim, no surrounding oedema, no enhancement, and gentle scalloping of the inner table of the skull. What is the lesion and how should the report frame it?
quiz.answer: A DNET, framed as a long-standing epileptogenic cortical lesion rather than an aggressive tumour
choices: A DNET, framed as a long-standing epileptogenic cortical lesion rather than an aggressive tumour
A ganglioglioma, framed around the enhancing mural nodule and calcification that characterise it
A cavernoma, framed around the complete haemosiderin rim and the blooming seen on susceptibility
An acute infarct, framed around the cortical swelling and restricted diffusion in a vascular territory
quiz.explain: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumours are cortically based, wedge-shaped or bubbly on T2, and characteristically have a bright FLAIR rim around a cluster of microcysts. They cause no oedema and little mass effect, and the slow remodelling of the overlying inner table testifies to how long they have been there. Enhancement is usually absent or faint. The reporting framing matters as much as the label: this is a lesion whose significance is seizures, so the report should support a planned epilepsy surgery pathway rather than trigger an urgent oncological work-up. A ganglioglioma, the other classic long-standing temporal lesion, more often shows a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule and calcification. A cavernoma would show a complete haemosiderin rim with marked blooming. An infarct would be territorial, swollen and diffusion-restricted, and would not scallop bone.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old with focal seizures has MRI showing smooth ovoid nodules lining both lateral ventricles. The nodules follow grey matter signal exactly on T1, T2 and FLAIR, do not enhance, and show no blooming on susceptibility imaging. What do you conclude and advise?
quiz.answer: Periventricular nodular heterotopia: grey matter in the wrong place, so no biopsy is needed
choices: Periventricular nodular heterotopia: grey matter in the wrong place, so no biopsy is needed
Subependymal nodules of tuberous sclerosis: look for calcification and cortical tubers as well
Subependymal tumour spread: the nodules would enhance and follow cerebrospinal fluid pathways
Old subependymal haemorrhage: blood products lining the ependymal surface after a preterm bleed
quiz.explain: The discriminator is signal, and the rule is simple: heterotopic grey matter is grey matter, so it matches cortex on every sequence, does not enhance, and does not bloom. Subependymal nodules in tuberous sclerosis often calcify and bloom, frequently enhance, and travel with cortical tubers and radial migration lines. Metastatic or lymphomatous subependymal deposits enhance and are usually irregular. Old germinal matrix haemorrhage leaves susceptibility-positive residue. Once heterotopia is established the useful work begins: describe how extensive and how symmetric the nodules are, look for the associated cortical malformation and for a thin corpus callosum or cerebellar hypoplasia, and mention that bilateral diffuse periventricular nodular heterotopia is associated with FLNA variants, since that carries implications for the patient's family as well as for surgical planning.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these investigations in the order a presurgical epilepsy programme would usually deploy them for a patient whose first MRI was reported as normal.
quiz.answer: HARNESS-MRI morphometric-post-processing FDG-PET ictal-SPECT intracranial-EEG
quiz.explain: The ladder climbs from cheap and non-invasive toward expensive and invasive, and each rung is only worth attempting once the one below it has been done properly. First repeat the structural study with a dedicated protocol, because a large share of so-called MRI-negative patients simply had the wrong sequences. Then run morphometric post-processing on the isotropic 3D T1, comparing junction and thickness maps against a normal database to flag candidate regions for a targeted re-read. Interictal FDG-PET follows, showing regional hypometabolism that usually extends beyond the lesion but reliably lateralises. Ictal SPECT, ideally coregistered with MRI, requires an injection during a seizure and is therefore resource-heavy and reserved for continuing uncertainty. Intracranial EEG sits at the top: it defines the seizure onset zone directly but carries surgical risk, and it needs a hypothesis to sample, which is precisely what every earlier rung supplies.

quiz.prompt: You are planning the dedicated coronal T2 stack. The hippocampus measures 4.0 cm along its long axis and you will use 2 mm slices with no interslice gap. How many slices are needed to cover it end to end? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Forty millimetres of coverage divided by 2 mm per contiguous slice gives 20 slices, and in practice you would prescribe a few more at each end so that the head and tail are not clipped. The planning point behind the arithmetic is that this stack must be angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis, prescribed on a sagittal or oblique reformat, and must run from in front of the hippocampal head to behind the tail. Coverage failures are a real cause of missed sclerosis, because the head is where the digitations live and the tail is where subtle atrophy declares itself. Thin contiguous slices also preserve the side-to-side comparison that the coronal plane exists to provide: symmetry is judged by looking at both hippocampi in the same slice, which an oblique or gapped acquisition quietly destroys.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old with focal seizures has a 12 mm lesion at the right frontal grey and white matter junction with a mixed-signal popcorn core and a complete dark rim on T2, blooming on gradient echo, with no oedema. A cousin had seizures and a brain haemorrhage. What do you add to the study and why?
quiz.answer: Whole-brain susceptibility-weighted imaging, to search for the additional lesions of the familial form
choices: Whole-brain susceptibility-weighted imaging, to search for the additional lesions of the familial form
Perfusion imaging through the lesion, to separate a cavernoma from a haemorrhagic metastatic deposit
Spectroscopy through the lesion, to demonstrate the choline elevation of a vascular malformation
Early and delayed contrast imaging, to demonstrate the rapid arteriovenous shunting that it contains
quiz.explain: The described lesion is a cavernous malformation: locules of blood of differing ages give the popcorn core, and the complete haemosiderin rim blooms heavily on susceptibility-sensitive sequences. With a family history the question is no longer what the lesion is but how many there are, because multiplicity defines familial cerebral cavernous malformation and changes counselling, surveillance and the genetic conversation for relatives. Susceptibility-weighted imaging is far more sensitive than gradient echo for the tiny punctate lesions that make the diagnosis, so it should cover the whole brain. Perfusion and spectroscopy add nothing to a lesion this characteristic. Cavernomas are angiographically occult and contain no arteriovenous shunt, so dynamic contrast imaging is misdirected, though it is worth looking for an associated developmental venous anomaly, which must be preserved if the cavernoma is resected.

quiz.prompt: Describe how polymicrogyria appears on a millimetric 3D T1 and name the associated finding that often accompanies it.
quiz.answer: The cortical ribbon looks irregular, stippled and overly folded, thin in reality but mimicking thickening at low resolution, most often around the sylvian fissure, and it is frequently accompanied by anomalous draining veins.
quiz.explain: Polymicrogyria is a disorder of late migration and cortical organisation in which many small gyri fuse at the surface. On a thick-slice study the packed miniature gyri average together and the cortical ribbon simply looks thick and lumpy, which is how it gets confused with pachygyria; on millimetric isotropic T1 the true stippled, bumpy inner surface with a shallow irregular sulcal pattern becomes visible. The perisylvian region is the commonest site, and bilateral perisylvian involvement produces a recognisable clinical syndrome with oromotor difficulty. Look for the companions: anomalous or enlarged draining veins over the affected cortex, an overlying arachnoid or subarachnoid space that appears too generous, and underlying white matter volume loss. Distribution matters for aetiology, since a unilateral perisylvian distribution raises congenital cytomegalovirus or an in utero vascular insult.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old with drug-resistant frontal lobe epilepsy has a full HARNESS protocol reported as normal. Scalp EEG and semiology both point to the right frontal lobe. What is the most useful next imaging step?
quiz.answer: Run morphometric post-processing against a normal database, then re-read with that hypothesis
choices: Run morphometric post-processing against a normal database, then re-read with that hypothesis
Report the study as normal and close the structural work-up before the surgical meeting is held
Repeat the identical MRI in twelve months and wait for the abnormality to declare itself over time
Rely on interictal FDG-PET alone and take the hypometabolic lobe as the resection target directly
quiz.explain: Around a quarter to a third of drug-resistant focal epilepsies are called MRI-negative, and a good share of those are really reader-negative: the lesion is on the images but is too subtle for an unguided read. Morphometric post-processing helps twice over. It builds junction, extension and thickness maps from the isotropic 3D T1 and compares them voxel by voxel against a normal cohort, generating candidate regions; and it then licenses a targeted second read, where a radiologist looks at one gyrus with the electroclinical hypothesis in hand. That combination converts a meaningful number of negative studies into positive ones, and finding the lesion improves the odds of seizure freedom after surgery. Simply repeating the same scan later rarely helps in an adult. FDG-PET is valuable but its hypometabolism is regional and typically wider than the lesion, so it lateralises rather than defines a resection margin.
